title: Islands: Land in the Middle of Water
summary: How islands form through volcanoes, coral, and separation from continents, with examples from around the world, and how living on an island differs from living on the mainland.
poll: Living on an island would be very different from living on the mainland.

versions.title: Land in the Middle of Water
versions.text:
An island is land. The ocean sits all around it. It can be big. It can be small.

Some islands grow from a volcano. It can sit deep under the sea. It can erupt. Hot rock shoots out. The rock cools off. It turns hard like stone. More hot rock piles on top. At last, it pokes above the waves. A new island is born! Hawaii grew this way.

Some islands grow from coral instead. Tiny bugs in the sea make it. Sand then piles on top. In time, it turns into an island.

Some islands were once part of a big land. The sea rose up high. It cut off one small piece. That piece then sat alone. It became its own island. Greenland grew this way.

Lots of islands sit close by the coast. They form one big group. Japan has small islands near it.

Life on an island can be hard. You may need a boat to leave. You may need a plane too. Big storms can hit the coast hard. Some small bugs live on just one island. They live there and no place else.

Life on an island can be quite different from life on land. People often need a boat or a plane to come and go. Big storms can hit the coast hard. Some plants and bugs live on just one island, and no place else.

versions.title: Land in the Middle of Water
versions.text:
An island is land that has ocean water on every side. Some islands are as big as a small country. Others are no bigger than just one bare rock near the coast.

Many islands grow from a volcano. It hides down under the sea floor. When such a volcano erupts, hot lava pours out. It cools off fast in the water. Bit by bit, layer after layer of lava piles up. After many years, the pile finally pokes above the waves. A brand-new island is born. The Hawaiian Islands grew in just this way, one eruption at a time.

Other islands grow from coral instead of lava. Along warm coasts, tiny sea bugs build hard coral. Waves along with fish slowly grind bits of it down into fine sand. Over many years, that sand piles up on top until it rises out of the water. It becomes a true island.

Some islands were once part of a much bigger land. When the sea rose, rising water covered over the lowest ground. It cut off just one piece of land from the land it had been joined to. That piece became its own island, cut off from its old neighbors. Greenland grew in a way very much like this.

Many islands sit close by each other near the coast. Japan has lots of islands grouped close together.

Life on an island is often quite different from life on land. People usually need a boat or a plane just to come and go. Storms can hit the coast hard, because there is no land nearby to block the wind. Some plants and animals that live on just one island live no place else on Earth.

versions.title: Land in the Middle of Water
versions.text:
An island is a piece of land completely surrounded by ocean water. Islands range in size from huge landmasses down to a single bare rock near a coastline.

Many islands form through volcanic action deep beneath the ocean floor. When an undersea volcano erupts, hot lava pours up through a crack in the seafloor. It cools fast in the cold water. Layer after layer of lava piles up on older rock. After many thousands of years, the mound finally breaks the surface. A brand-new island is formed. The Hawaiian Islands formed through this same process, one eruption at a time.

Other islands are built by coral rather than lava. Along warm coasts, tiny sea animals build hard coral. Waves and fish slowly grind bits of it, through natural erosion, into fine sand. Over many years, that sand piles up until it rises above the water and becomes a true island, with its own habitat for birds.

Some islands were once part of a much bigger land before being cut off from it. When sea levels rose after the last ice age, rising water covered low ground. It cut off a piece of land from the land it had been joined to. That piece became an island on its own, cut off from its old neighbors. Greenland formed in roughly this way.

Many islands cluster in a group called an archipelago. Japan is a large archipelago made of many separate islands.

Life on an island often differs from life on the mainland. Since there is no road connecting an island to anywhere else, people rely on boats or planes just to come and go. Storms can hit the coast hard, since no land nearby blocks the wind. Because islands sit isolated in the ocean, many living things that grew up there live nowhere else on Earth.

versions.title: Worlds Apart: How Islands Rise from the Sea
versions.text:
An island is a piece of land entirely surrounded by ocean water, ranging in size from enormous landmasses to a single remote rock near a coastline. Every island, large or small, is isolated from other land by the water around it.

Many islands form through volcanic activity deep beneath the ocean floor, often along tectonic boundaries where plates of the Earth's crust meet. When an undersea volcano erupts, molten lava forces its way through a crack in the seafloor and hardens into solid rock. Layer after layer of lava builds up over thousands of years, until the mound finally breaks the surface and a new island is born. The Hawaiian Islands formed this way, as a single hot spot produced one eruption after another across millions of years.

Other islands owe their existence to coral rather than to tectonic forces. Along warm coastlines, tiny marine animals build coral reefs, while waves and fish grind pieces of the reef into fine sand. Over many years, that sand piles up on the reef until it rises above the water and becomes an island with its own habitat.

Still other islands, called continental islands, were once part of a larger landmass before being separated from it. When sea levels rose after the last ice age, rising water cut off a piece of land from the mainland it had been joined to. Greenland and the British Isles both formed in roughly this way, after the connecting land failed to subside into a lasting bridge.

Many islands cluster together within a group called an archipelago. Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines are archipelagos made up of thousands of separate islands.

Life on an island frequently differs from life on the mainland. Because no road connects a remote island to anywhere else, people depend on boats or airplanes to come and go, which can make supplies more costly. Storms can batter the coastline with particular force, since no inland terrain exists to block the wind. Because islands remain isolated, many species that evolved there became endemic, meaning they exist nowhere else on the planet.

versions.title: Worlds Apart: How Islands Rise from the Sea
versions.text:
An island is a piece of land entirely surrounded by ocean water, ranging in size from enormous landmasses to a single remote rock rising precipitously near a coastline. Every island, whatever its size, is isolated from other land by the water that encircles it.

Many islands form through volcanic activity deep beneath the ocean floor, often along tectonic boundaries where plates of the Earth's crust collide or pull apart. When an undersea volcano erupts, molten lava forces its way through a crack in the seafloor and hardens into solid basaltic rock. Layer after layer of lava builds up over thousands of years, until the mound finally breaches the surface and a new island is born. The Hawaiian Islands formed this way, as a stationary hot spot produced one eruption after another while the crust slowly drifted above it.

Other islands owe their existence to coral rather than to tectonic forces. Along warm, shallow coastlines, tiny marine animals build coral reefs, while waves together with fish grind fragments of the reef into fine sand. Over many years, that sand accumulates on the reef until it rises above the water and becomes an island with its own distinct habitat.

Still other islands, known as continental islands, were once part of a larger landmass before being separated from it entirely. When sea levels rose after the last ice age, rising water cut off a piece of continental crust from the mainland it had been joined to. Greenland and the British Isles both came into existence in roughly this manner, since the connecting land failed to subside into a stable bridge.

Many islands cluster together within a group known as an archipelago. Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines are all archipelagos made up of thousands of separate islands.

Life on an island frequently differs from life on the mainland. Because no road connects a remote island to anywhere else, residents depend on boats or airplanes to come and go, which can make basic supplies considerably more costly. Storms tend to batter the coastline with particular force, since no inland terrain exists nearby to block the wind. Because islands remain isolated within the ocean, many species that evolved there became endemic, meaning they exist nowhere else on the planet.

versions.title: Worlds Apart: How Islands Rise from the Sea
versions.text:
An island is a piece of land entirely surrounded by ocean or sea water, ranging in size from enormous landmasses to a single remote rock rising precipitously near a coastline. Regardless of size, every island shares one defining characteristic: tectonic and oceanic forces have rendered it isolated from other land by the water that encircles it on every side.

Many islands form through volcanic activity occurring deep beneath the ocean floor, frequently along tectonic boundaries where enormous plates of the Earth's crust collide, slide past one another, or gradually pull apart. When an undersea volcano erupts, molten rock known as lava forces its way through a fissure in the seafloor, cools rapidly upon contact with the surrounding cold water, and hardens into solid basaltic rock. Layer after layer of lava and ash gradually accumulate atop older material, and after many thousands of years the growing mound eventually breaches the surface, creating an entirely new island. The Hawaiian Islands formed through precisely this process, as a stationary hot spot deep within the mantle produced one volcanic eruption after another while the crust above it slowly drifted across millions of years, leaving a chain of islands in its wake.

Other islands owe their existence to coral rather than to tectonic forces. Along warm, shallow coastlines, tiny marine animals construct hard coral reefs, while waves together with coral-eating fish gradually grind fragments of the reef through natural erosion into fine sand. Over many years, that sand accumulates atop the reef until it eventually rises above the waterline and becomes a genuine island, complete with its own distinct habitat supporting birds, insects, and coastal plants found nowhere else nearby.

Still other islands, known as continental islands, were once part of a far larger landmass before being separated from it entirely. When sea levels rose following the last ice age, the rising water submerged low-lying ground and severed a piece of continental crust from the mainland to which it had previously been joined. That piece became an island in its own right, permanently isolated from the neighbors with which it once shared a single coastline. Greenland and the British Isles both came into existence in roughly this manner, as melting glaciers raised the surrounding seas while the connecting land failed to subside into a permanent, stable land bridge.

Many islands cluster together within a group known as an archipelago. Japan, Indonesia, and the Philippines are all archipelagos composed of thousands of separate islands scattered across the surrounding sea, each supporting its own particular habitat and community of living things.

Life on an island frequently differs sharply from life on the mainland. Because no road connects a remote island to anywhere else, residents typically depend on boats or airplanes simply to come and go, a reality that can make basic supplies considerably more expensive. Storms tend to batter the coastline with particular force, since no substantial inland terrain exists nearby to block the wind before it arrives. Because islands remain isolated within the ocean, many species that evolved there became endemic, meaning they exist naturally nowhere else on the planet.

versions.title: Worlds Apart: How Islands Rise from the Sea
versions.text:
An island, by definition, is a piece of land entirely surrounded by ocean or sea water, and islands range enormously in scale, from landmasses nearly the size of small continents down to a single remote rock rising precipitously near an otherwise unremarkable coastline. Regardless of size, however, every island shares one defining characteristic: tectonic and oceanic forces have rendered it permanently isolated from other land by the water that encircles it on every side, a condition with far-reaching consequences for the plants, animals, and people who make their homes there.

A great many islands owe their existence to volcanic activity occurring deep beneath the ocean floor, frequently along tectonic boundaries where enormous plates of the Earth's crust collide, slide past one another, or gradually pull apart. When an undersea volcano erupts, molten rock known as lava forces its way through a fissure in the seafloor, cools rapidly upon contact with the surrounding cold water, and hardens into solid basaltic rock; layer after layer of lava and ash then accumulate atop this older material until, after many thousands of years, the growing mound finally breaches the surface and an entirely new island is born. The Hawaiian Islands formed through precisely this process, as a stationary hot spot deep within the planet's mantle produced one volcanic eruption after another while the crust above it slowly drifted across millions of years, leaving behind an entire chain of islands strung out across the Pacific in its wake.

A second group of islands owes its existence not to tectonic forces but to coral. Along warm, shallow coastlines, countless tiny marine animals construct hard coral reefs, while waves and coral-eating fish gradually grind fragments of those reefs, through a slow process of natural erosion, into fine sand; over many years this sand accumulates atop the reef until it eventually rises above the waterline and becomes a genuine island, complete with its own distinct habitat capable of supporting birds, insects, and coastal plants that could never survive out on the open water.

A third kind of island, known as a continental island, was once simply part of a far larger landmass before being separated from it entirely. When global sea levels rose dramatically following the last ice age, the rising water submerged low-lying ground and severed a piece of continental crust from the mainland to which it had previously been joined, leaving that piece permanently isolated as an island in its own right. Greenland and the British Isles both came into being in roughly this manner, formed when melting glaciers raised the surrounding seas while the connecting land in between failed to subside gradually enough to remain a stable, permanent bridge.

Many islands cluster together within a group known as an archipelago, such as Japan, Indonesia, or the Philippines, each composed of thousands of separate islands scattered across the surrounding sea and each supporting its own particular habitat and community of living things that may differ quite noticeably even from one neighboring island to the next.

Life on an island, in nearly every respect, differs sharply from life on the mainland. Because no road connects a remote island to anywhere else, residents typically depend entirely on boats or airplanes simply to come and go, a reality that tends to make basic supplies considerably more expensive and travel considerably slower than it would be on a continent. Storms, moreover, tend to batter island coastlines with particular ferocity, since no substantial inland terrain exists nearby to slow the wind before it arrives. Because islands remain isolated within the ocean for such long stretches of time, many of the species that evolved there eventually became endemic, meaning they exist naturally nowhere else on the entire planet, a fact that renders island habitats both extraordinarily precious and extraordinarily vulnerable to any sudden disturbance.

versions.title: Worlds Apart: How Islands Rise from the Sea
versions.text:
An island, by strict definition, is a piece of land entirely surrounded by ocean or sea water, and islands range enormously in scale, from landmasses nearly the size of small continents down to a single remote rock rising precipitously out of an otherwise unremarkable stretch of coastline. Regardless of size, however, every island shares one defining characteristic: tectonic and oceanic forces have rendered it permanently and irreversibly isolated from other land by the water that encircles it on every conceivable side, a condition with far-reaching consequences for the plants, animals, and people who ultimately make their homes there.

A great many islands owe their existence to volcanic activity occurring deep beneath the ocean floor, frequently along tectonic boundaries where enormous plates of the Earth's crust collide, slide past one another, or gradually pull apart over immense stretches of geological time. When an undersea volcano erupts, molten rock known as lava forces its way through a fissure in the seafloor, cools almost instantly upon contact with the surrounding cold water, and hardens into solid basaltic rock; layer after layer of lava and ash then accumulate atop this older material until, after many thousands of years, the slowly growing mound finally breaches the surface and an entirely new island is born. The Hawaiian Islands formed through precisely this process, as a stationary hot spot situated deep within the planet's mantle produced one volcanic eruption after another while the crust above it drifted gradually across millions upon millions of years, leaving behind an entire chain of islands strung out across the vast expanse of the Pacific Ocean in its wake.

A second, entirely distinct group of islands owes its existence not to tectonic forces at all but rather to coral. Along warm, shallow coastlines, countless tiny marine animals laboriously construct hard coral reefs, while waves and coral-eating fish gradually grind fragments of those same reefs, through an unhurried process of natural erosion, into exceptionally fine sand; over many years this sand steadily accumulates atop the reef until it eventually rises above the waterline altogether and becomes a genuine island, complete with its own distinct habitat capable of supporting birds, insects, and coastal plants that could never otherwise survive out on the open water.

A third and final kind of island, known formally as a continental island, was once simply an integral part of a far larger landmass before being separated from it entirely by forces beyond its control. When global sea levels rose dramatically following the conclusion of the last ice age, the rising water gradually submerged low-lying ground and severed a piece of continental crust from the mainland to which it had previously and continuously been joined, leaving that piece permanently isolated as an island in its own right. Greenland and the British Isles both came into being in roughly this manner, formed when melting glaciers raised the surrounding seas while the connecting land in between failed to subside gradually enough to remain a stable, permanent land bridge indefinitely.

Many islands cluster together within a larger group known as an archipelago, such as Japan, Indonesia, or the Philippines, each composed of thousands upon thousands of separate islands scattered widely across the surrounding sea and each supporting its own particular, often subtly distinct habitat and community of living things that may differ quite noticeably even from one neighboring island to the very next.

Life on an island, in nearly every conceivable respect, tends to differ sharply and often unexpectedly from life on the mainland. Because no road connects a remote island to anywhere else whatsoever, residents typically depend entirely and unavoidably on boats or airplanes simply to come and go, a persistent reality that tends to make even basic supplies considerably more expensive and ordinary travel considerably slower than it would otherwise be on a continuous continent. Storms, moreover, tend to batter island coastlines with particular and often devastating ferocity, since no substantial inland terrain exists anywhere nearby to slow the wind's advance before it finally arrives. Because islands remain so thoroughly isolated within the ocean across such long stretches of time, a great many of the species that gradually evolved there eventually became endemic, meaning they exist naturally nowhere else whatsoever on the entire planet, a fact that renders island habitats both extraordinarily precious and extraordinarily vulnerable to any sudden, unforeseen disturbance.

Why coral reefs have so many colorful fish and plants

HIGH.modelAnswer: Volcanic islands form along tectonic boundaries, where undersea volcanoes erupt lava that cools and builds up over thousands of years until it breaks the surface. Coral islands form when tiny marine animals build reefs that waves and fish slowly erode into sand, which accumulates until it rises above the water, while continental islands form when rising sea levels separate a piece of continental crust from the mainland, as happened with Greenland and the British Isles. Because islands remain isolated from other land for such long periods, many species that evolve there become endemic, existing naturally nowhere else on the planet.
